title: Chapter 4. Of Speech
paragraphs: Printing, though an ingenious invention, is no great matter compared with the invention of letters. Who first discovered the use of letters is unknown. The man who first brought them into Greece, men say, was Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of Phoenicia. It was a useful invention for preserving the memory of times past and for binding together a mankind dispersed across so many distant regions of the earth — and a difficult one too, since it required close observation of the various motions of the tongue, palate, lips, and the other organs of speech, in order to mark each one with its own character. But the most noble and useful invention of all was speech itself, made up of names (or appellations) and their connection, by which men record their thoughts, recall them when they are past, and declare them to one another for mutual use and conversation. Without speech there would have been no commonwealth, no society, no contract, and no peace among men — no more than there is among lions, bears, and wolves. The first author of speech was God himself, who instructed Adam how to name the creatures he set before his eyes; for Scripture goes no further in this matter. But that much was enough to direct Adam to add more names as the experience and use of things gave him occasion, and to join them, step by step, in ways that made him understood. By this slow accumulation, over time, he gathered as much language as he found use for — though not as copious as an orator or philosopher needs. For I find nothing in Scripture from which we can directly or by consequence gather that Adam was taught the names of all figures, numbers, measures, colours, sounds, fancies, or relations — much less the grammatical names of words and speech, such as General, Special, Affirmative, Negative, Interrogative, Optative, Infinitive, all of which are useful; and least of all the words Entity, Intentionality, Quiddity, and the other significant terms of the Schools.

But all that language, gathered and expanded by Adam and his descendants, was lost again at the tower of Babel, when by God's hand every man was struck, for his rebellion, with forgetfulness of his former tongue. Driven thereby to scatter themselves into the various parts of the world, it could only be that the present diversity of tongues proceeded by degrees from that scattering — taught to each people, as need (the mother of all inventions) required, and growing more copious with time.

The general use of speech is to translate our mental discourse into verbal discourse — to turn the train of our thoughts into a train of words — and this serves two purposes. The first is to record the consequences of our thoughts, which would otherwise slip from memory and force us to do the work again; words allow them to be recalled by the marks they were tied to. In this first use, names serve as marks, or notes of remembrance. The second purpose comes when many people use the same words to signify, by their order and connection, what they conceive or think about each matter, and likewise what they desire, fear, or feel any other passion about; in this use, words are called signs. The special uses of speech are these. First, to record what we find, by reflection, to be the cause of anything present or past, and what we find present or past things may produce or bring about — which, in sum, is the acquiring of the arts. Second, to show others the knowledge we have attained — that is, to counsel and teach one another. Third, to make known to others our wills and intentions, so that we may have one another's mutual help. Fourth, to please and amuse ourselves and others by playing with our words, innocently, for pleasure or ornament.

To these uses there correspond four abuses. First, when men record their thoughts wrongly, through the inconstancy of the meaning of their words, and so register as their conception something they never actually conceived, deceiving themselves. Second, when they use words metaphorically — that is, in a sense other than the one those words were appointed for — and so deceive others. Third, when they declare with words that to be their will which is not. Fourth, when they use words to wound one another. For since nature has armed living creatures — some with teeth, some with horns, some with hands — to wound an enemy, it is only an abuse of speech to wound a man with the tongue; unless he is one whom we are obliged to govern, in which case it is not to wound but to correct and amend.
The way speech serves the remembrance of the consequence of causes and effects lies in the imposition of names, and in their connection.

Of names, some are proper — peculiar to one thing only — such as Peter, John, this man, this tree; and some are common to many things, such as man, horse, tree. Each of these, though only one name, is nevertheless the name of various particular things; and in respect of all of them taken together, it is called a universal. There is nothing universal in the world but names; the things named are every one of them individual and singular.

A universal name is imposed on many things because they resemble one another in some quality or other accident. And whereas a proper name brings to mind one thing only, a universal recalls any one of those many things.

Among universal names, some have wider and some narrower meaning, the wider taking in the narrower; some are of equal extent and take in each other reciprocally. For example, the name Body is wider than the word Man, and contains it; the names Man and Rational are of equal extent and contain one another. But here we must take notice that by a 'name' we do not always mean, as in grammar, one word only, but sometimes several words taken together as a circumlocution. All these words — He That In His Actions Observes The Laws Of His Country — make up a single name, equivalent to the one word Just.

By imposing names of wider or narrower significance, we turn the reckoning of the consequences of things imagined in the mind into a reckoning of the consequences of names. For example: a man who has no use of speech at all — one born and remaining perfectly deaf and dumb — if he sets a triangle before his eyes alongside two right angles (such as the corners of a square), may by reflection find that the three angles of that triangle equal the two right angles standing beside it. But if another triangle of a different shape is then shown to him, he cannot know without a fresh effort whether the three angles of that one are also equal to the same. By contrast, a man who has the use of words, once he notices that this equality followed not from the length of the sides, nor from any other particular feature of his triangle, but only from this — that the sides were straight and the angles three; and that this was all that made him call it a triangle — will boldly conclude, universally, that the same equality of angles holds in all triangles whatsoever, and will record his finding in these general terms: Every Triangle Has Its Three Angles Equal To Two Right Angles. In this way the consequence found in one particular case comes to be registered and remembered as a universal rule; our mental reckoning is discharged of time and place; we are spared all labour of the mind except the first; and what was found true Here and Now becomes true at All Times and in All Places.

The use of words for recording our thoughts is in nothing more evident than in counting. A natural fool, who could never learn the order of the numeral words — One, Two, Three — may note every stroke of the clock and nod at it, or say 'one, one, one,' but can never know what hour it strikes. There was, it seems, a time when those number-names were not yet in use, and men were forced to apply the fingers of one or both hands to the things they wanted to keep account of; this is plausibly why our numeral words, in any nation, run only to ten — in some only to five — and then begin again. And he who can count to ten, if he recites them out of order, will lose himself and not know when he is done. Much less will he be able to add, to subtract, or to carry out any of the other operations of arithmetic. So without words there is no possibility of reckoning numbers — much less of reckoning magnitudes, speeds, forces, and other things whose calculation is necessary to the being or the well-being of mankind.

When two names are joined together into a consequence, or affirmation — as in 'A man is a living creature,' or 'If he is a man, he is a living creature' — if the later name (living creature) signifies all that the former name (man) signifies, then the affirmation, or the consequence, is true; otherwise it is false. For true and false are attributes of speech, not of things. Where there is no speech, there is neither truth nor falsehood. There may be error — as when we expect what will not come, or suspect what has not been — but in neither of those cases can a man be charged with untruth.

Since truth then consists in the right ordering of names within our affirmations, a man who seeks precise truth must remember what each name he uses stands for, and place it accordingly — or else he will find himself entangled in his words, like a bird in lime-twigs: the more he struggles, the more he is stuck. This is why in geometry — the only science that it has so far pleased God to grant to mankind — men begin by settling the meanings of their words; this settling of meanings they call Definitions, and they place them at the very beginning of their reckoning.

From this it appears how necessary it is, for any man who aspires to true knowledge, to examine the definitions of earlier authors — either correcting them where they are carelessly set down, or making them himself. For errors in definitions multiply as the reckoning proceeds, and lead men into absurdities which at last they see but cannot avoid, unless they reckon again from the beginning, where the foundation of their errors lies. Hence it happens that those who trust to books do as men do who cast up many little sums into a great one, without considering whether those little sums were rightly cast up to begin with: when at last the error becomes visible, since they do not suspect their first grounds, they do not know how to clear themselves, but spend their time fluttering through their books — like birds that, entering by the chimney and finding themselves shut in a chamber, beat themselves against the false light of a glass window for want of wit to consider which way they came in. So the first use of speech lies in the right defining of names — which is the acquiring of science; and the first abuse lies in wrong definitions, or none at all — from which proceed all the false and senseless tenets that make those men who take their instruction from the authority of books, rather than from their own reflection, fall as far below the condition of ignorant men as men endowed with true science stand above it. For between true science and erroneous doctrine, ignorance is in the middle. Natural sense and imagination are not subject to absurdity; nature itself cannot err; and as men grow in abundance of language, they become either wiser than ordinary or madder than ordinary. Nor is it possible, without letters, for any man to become either excellently wise, or (unless his memory is damaged by disease, or by some defect of the organs) excellently foolish. For words are wise men's counters — they only reckon with them; but they are the money of fools, who value them by the authority of an Aristotle, a Cicero, a Thomas, or any other doctor whatever, so long as he is a man.

Whatever can enter into an account or be considered in a reckoning is subject to names — whatever can be added to another to make a sum, or subtracted from another to leave a remainder. The Latins called accounts of money rationes, and the activity of accounting ratiocinatio; what we, in bills or account books, call items they called nomina — that is, names; and from this, it seems, they extended the word ratio to the faculty of reckoning in everything else. The Greeks have only one word, logos, for both speech and reason — not because they thought there was no speech without reason, but because there is no reasoning without speech. The act of reasoning they called syllogism, which means summing up the consequences of one statement with another. And because the same things may enter into the account under different aspects, their names are (to show that variety) twisted and diversified. This diversity of names can be reduced to four general heads.

First, a thing may enter into the account as matter, or body — as Living, Sensible, Rational, Hot, Cold, Moved, Quiet — in all of which the word matter or body is understood. All such are names of matter.

Second, a thing may enter into the account, or be considered, in respect of some accident or quality we conceive to be in it: as Being Moved, Being So Long, Being Hot, and so on. Then, by a small change or twist on the name of the thing itself, we make a name for that accident which we are considering: for Living we put into the account Life; for Moved, Motion; for Hot, Heat; for Long, Length, and so on. All such names are names of the accidents and properties by which one matter, or body, is distinguished from another. These are called abstract names — because they are severed (not from matter, but) from the account of matter.

Third, we bring into the account the properties of our own bodies, by which we make this kind of distinction: when something is seen by us, we do not reckon the thing itself, but the sight, the colour, the idea of it in the imagination; when something is heard, we do not reckon the thing itself, but the hearing, or the sound, which is our conception of it through the ear. These are names of fancies.

Fourth, we bring into the account, consider, and give names to names themselves and to speeches. So General, Universal, Special, Equivocal are names of names. And Affirmation, Interrogation, Command, Narration, Syllogism, Sermon, Oration, and many other such terms, are names of speeches.

And this exhausts the variety of positive names — names imposed to mark something that exists in nature, or may be conceived by the mind of man: bodies that exist or may be conceived, the properties of bodies that exist or may be imagined, or words and speech.

There are also other names, called negative, which are marks that signify that a given word is not the name of the thing in question — such words as Nothing, No Man, Infinite, Inteachable, Three Want Four, and the like. These are still useful in reckoning, or in the correction of reckoning: they call to mind our past thoughts, even though they are not names of anything, because they make us refuse to admit names that are not rightly used.

All other names are merely insignificant sounds, and they come in two kinds. The first is when they are new, and yet their meaning has not been explained by definition. The Schoolmen and confused philosophers have coined plenty of these.

The second kind comes when men compound a name out of two names whose meanings are contradictory and inconsistent — such as the name an Incorporeal Body, or (the same thing) an Incorporeal Substance, and many more. For whenever an affirmation is false, the two names composing it, joined together into one, signify nothing at all. For example, if it is a false affirmation to say A Quadrangle Is Round, then the phrase Round Quadrangle signifies nothing — it is a mere sound. So too, if it is false to say that virtue can be poured, or blown up and down, then the phrases Infused Virtue or Inspired Virtue are as absurd and meaningless as Round Quadrangle. And you will hardly meet with a senseless and insignificant word that is not built out of some Latin or Greek term. A Frenchman seldom hears our Saviour called by the name Parole, but very often by the name Verbe — yet Verbe and Parole differ only in that one is Latin and the other French.

When a man, upon hearing a piece of speech, has those thoughts which the words of that speech, and their connection, were appointed and constituted to signify, then he is said to understand it — understanding being nothing but conception produced by speech. Therefore, if speech is peculiar to man (as, for all I know, it is), then understanding is peculiar to him as well. And so, for absurd and false affirmations, when they are universal, there can be no understanding — though many think they understand when they really only repeat the words quietly, or rehearse them in their mind.
What kinds of speech signify the appetites, aversions, and passions of the human mind, and the use and abuse of them, I shall treat when I have spoken of the passions themselves.

The names of those things that affect us — those that please and displease us — are of inconstant meaning in everyday conversation, because not all men are affected the same way by the same thing, nor is the same man at all times. For since all names are imposed to signify our conceptions, and all our affections are nothing but conceptions, then when we conceive the same things differently we can hardly avoid naming them differently. The nature of what we conceive may be the same; yet the variety in our reception of it — given different bodily constitutions and the prejudices of opinion — colours everything with the tincture of our own passions. And so in reasoning a man must beware of words which, besides signifying what we imagine of the nature of things, also signify the disposition and interest of the speaker — such as the names of virtues and vices. One man calls 'wisdom' what another calls 'fear'; one calls 'cruelty' what another calls 'justice'; one 'prodigality' what another 'magnanimity'; one 'gravity' what another 'stupidity'; and so on. Such names can never serve as true grounds of reasoning. Nor can metaphors and figures of speech — though these are less dangerous, because they openly profess their inconstancy, which the others do not.
